item.title: [NH] NH Education Deep Dive — The Burden Shift: How HB 581 Rewrote the Rules of Special Ed Disputes in New Hampshire
item.description:
In 2021, New Hampshire moved the burden of proof in special education due process hearings off of parents and onto school districts. Alex and Jordan break down HB 581 — what changed, what it means for parents and districts, and what it demands of NH special education teams in their daily work. Educational guidance, not legal advice.
Work with our consultant One-on-one help for parents from an NH special education administrator: IEP reviews, meeting prep, Prior Written Notice — what to ask for, and how to ask for it. Consults $250 — book a consult: [link]
Sources - HB 581 as introduced (2021), full bill text (PDF), NH General Court archives: https://gencourt.state.nh.us/BillHistory/SofS_Archives/2021/house/HB581H.pdf - RSA 186-C:16-b, current text — Due Process Hearing; Appeal (see paragraph III-a), official NH General Court statute site: https://www.GenCourt.state.nh.us/rsa/html/XV/186-C/186-C-mrg.htm - "NH Changes Law Regarding Burden of Proof in Special Education Due Process Hearings," Disability Rights Center–New Hampshire, Aug 2, 2021: https://drcnh.org/statements/burden-of-proof-in-due-process-hearings/ - "Sununu signs bill shifting burden of proof in special education hearings to schools," Keene Sentinel (via NH Bulletin), 2021: https://www.keenesentinel.com/news/local/sununu-signs-bill-shifting-burden-of-proof-in-special-education-hearings-to-schools/article_78864d50-12bb-5eac-8d49-78cb31042cbf.html - NH Department of Education, FY26 "Rules and Laws in Excess" chart (PDF): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/fy26-nh-rules-and-laws-in-excess-chart.pdf - 2025 Compilation of Education Legislation, NH School Boards Association (PDF) — includes HB 754 (automatic discovery): https://nhsba.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/2025-Compilation-of-Ed-Legislation-for-2025-Legislative-Summary.pdf - "New Hampshire Shifted the Due Process Burden to Schools in IEP Disputes. item.title: [New Hampshire] Deep Dive — State Complaints, ESY, and Compensatory Education
item.description:
This deep dive walks through the three dispute tools that meet in one file folder: the state complaint under 34 CFR 300.151 through 300.153 and New Hampshire's Ed 1121 process (who can file, the sixty-day clock, the commissioner's signed decision, the twenty-day reconsideration rule, and the public complaint summaries required by RSA 186-C:5-a); extended school year under 34 CFR 300.106 and New Hampshire's Ed 1110.01 (individual team determination, the regression and recoupment standard, and the factors beyond regression); and compensatory education under the qualitative "but for" standard of Reid v. District of Columbia, 401 F.3d 516 (D.C. Cir. 2005), including the First Circuit's Pihl decision and real New Hampshire complaint orders that required districts to deliver compensatory services. The episode closes with the documentation habits that decide these cases in practice. item.title: The Plan Nobody Audits: Section 504's Quiet Quadrupling
item.description:
This deep dive examines the fastest-growing accommodation system in American public schools: plans under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 held by students who do not have IEPs. Drawing on the U.S. Department of Education's Civil Rights Data Collection for 2023–24 and the leading published research, Alex and Jordan walk through what a Section 504 plan is and how its three-part eligibility test differs from the IDEA; how the "504-only" rate climbed from 1.1% of students in 2009–10 to 3.9% in 2021–22 and about 1.9 million students (4%) in 2023–24; why rates range from near double the national average in Texas and New Hampshire to below half in New Mexico and Mississippi, with individual Texas middle schools above 30% and other schools at zero; the documented skew toward White students (60% of 504-only students against 44% of enrollment) and, in the first study to link school records to IRS tax data, toward higher-income families (2.9% vs. 1.5%), even as IEPs run the opposite way; the measured response of 504 enrollment to the College Board's 2017 decision to honor school accommodations on the SAT automatically; the costs of both over-identification and under-identification; and the central evidentiary gap — no national breakdown of 504 plans by condition and no national audit of 504 eligibility has ever been published, so claims about how many plans are "unnecessary" exceed what the evidence can support. Plain-English explanations, with every number sourced and the limits of the evidence stated on air.
### Sources
- U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights, "A First Look: The Civil Rights Data Collection, 2023–24" (September 2026) — 19% of students with disabilities (15% IDEA; 4% / ~1.9M Section 504 only); White students 60% of 504-only vs. 44% of enrollment; boys 56% of 504-only: https://www.ed.gov/media/document/2023-24-first-look-civil-rights-data-collection-september-30-2026-114593.pdf - Perry A. Zirkel, "Concerns About Misidentification of '504-Only' Students," ATPE News, March 30, 2026 — 1.1% (2009–10) to 3.9% (2021–22); Texas 7.6%; 23 of the top 25 districts (14.4%–17.4%); Texas middle schools at 23.1%–30.1%; three-part eligibility test; no federal/state funding; costs of over- and under-identification; Texas dyslexia analysis: https://atpenews.org/concerns-about-misidentification-of-504-only-students/ - Perry A. Zirkel, "Mis-identifying '504-Only' Students," eSchool News, February 6, 2026 — New Hampshire and Texas at almost double the national rate; New Mexico and Mississippi at less than half; California 2.1% with districts ranging 0%–13.9% and schools 0%–24.2%: https://www.eschoolnews.com/innovative-teaching/2026/02/06/mis-identifying-504-only-students/ - Zirkel et al., analysis of the 2009–10 Civil Rights Data Collection, Journal of Disability Policy Studies (2014), reported by Education Week — 504-only rates: White 1.26%, Black 0.57%, Hispanic 0.50%; item.title: The List Nobody Can See: Inside the Child Care Food Program's Seven-Year Blacklist
item.description:
One routine Federal Register notice this fall renewed the paperwork behind the National Disqualified List — the Child and Adult Care Food Program's national bar on institutions, sponsoring organizations, day care home providers, and the individuals who run them. This deep dive opens up the machine: how a review finding becomes a "serious deficiency," how the corrective-action clock runs, why quitting does not save you, the appeal you get — and the six decisions 7 CFR 226.6(k)(3) says you can never appeal — and how a listing lasts seven years, or longer if a program debt is unpaid. Plus the vagueness problem the National CACFP Association put in writing (the same citation can mean a serious management problem in one state or "three small errors on a reimbursement claims form" in another), the patchwork early-removal door, the Feeding Our Future record that explains why the list exists, and the 2024 proposed rule (FNS-2024-0005) that would rebuild the process — still unfinalized. USDA does not publish the list or its size; where the public record runs out, this episode says so.
Sources: - 7 CFR 226.6 (CACFP State agency responsibilities — serious deficiency process at (c), National Disqualified List at (c)(7), administrative review at (k), day care home reviews at (l)): https://www.casemine.com/regulation/us/640f05fa8b0a3c5be33657ac/amp (also available at eCFR, Title 7, Part 226, §226.6) - USDA Food and Nutrition Service, "Proposed Rule: Serious Deficiency Process in the CACFP and SFSP" (docket FNS-2024-0005; comments due May 21, 2024; page updated February 4, 2026): https://fns-prod.azureedge.us/cn/fr-022124 - Proposed rule as published, 89 FR 13150 (February 21, 2024): https://www.cacfp.org/assets/pdf/SD+Propsoed+Rule+FR+Document+2024-02108/ - National CACFP Association (National CACFP Sponsors Association), comment letter on FNS-2024-0005, May 17, 2024 (signed Lisa Mack, President & CEO): https://files.constantcontact.com/e5582ed6201/f25b5196-65c4-4976-9cad-8cd96d1c625c.pdf - National CACFP Association, "NCA Response – National Disqualified List Information Collection," August 5, 2026: https://www.cacfp.org/2026/08/05/nca-response-national-disqualified-list-information-collection/ - National CACFP Association, Quarterly Policy Update, October 2026 (NDL information-collection comment summary): https://www.cacfp.org/2026/10/07/quarterly-policy-update-october-2026/ - USDA Food and Nutrition Service, "Why CACFP Is Important" (program scale and authority): https://fns-prod.azureedge.us/cacfp/why-cacfp-important - California Department of Social Services, CACFP "National Disqualified List" (state submission requirements for NDL entries): http://www.cdss.ca.gov/cacfp/resources/national-disqualified-list - California Department of Social Services, CACFP monitoring requirements (serious deficiency consequences under §226.6(c)(3)(ii)(O)): https://cdss.ca.gov/cacfp/resources/cacfp-monitoring-requirements-for-participation - U.S. Department of Justice, "St. Paul Man Sentenced to 33 Months' Imprisonment for Defrauding $1.6 Million in Federal Child Nutrition Program Funds" (Feeding Our Future), October 2026: https://www.justice.gov/usao-mn/pr/st-paul-man-sentenced-33-months-imprisonment-defrauding-16-million-federal-child - Tennessee Department of Human Services, "Joint State and Federal Investigation Stops Food Program Fraud" (Memphis CACFP case): https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/news/2021/7/16/joint-state-and-federal-investigation-stops-food-program-fraud.html - Federal Register notice 2026-21613 (CACFP National Disqualified List information collection, 2026 renewal cycle — 60-day notice published June 2026; comment period ended August 17, 2026): no stable URL retrieved; search federalregister.gov for "Agency Information Collection Activities: Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) National Disqualified List" and filter to 2026 Food and Nutrition Service notices. - Serious Deficiency, Suspension, and Appeals Handbook (FNS/state agency handbook referenced for early-removal practice): https://snp.ade.arkansas.gov/PDFArchive/USDA%20Memos/CACFP_Serious_Deficiency_Handbook%20%202%2010%202015.pdf - KidKare, "CACFP Serious Deficiency Process: 2026 Sponsor Guide" (FNS January 2026 state-agency webinar summary): https://www.kidkare.com/cacfp-serious-deficiency-process-sponsor-guide/

item.title: [North Carolina] District Deep Dive — Wake County Public School System

Sources: - WCPSS 2025-26 Adopted Budget (enrollment 161,115, county appropriation $741,944,152, per-student allocation $4,079): https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1765391024/wcpssnet/cqqyo4warulqa6xsnj0h/2025-26AdoptedBudget.pdf - item.title: [Maine] Education Trends — Chronic Absenteeism: One in Four Students, and the Long Climb Back
item.description:
One in four Maine students is chronically absent — the rate fell from a 31.1 percent pandemic peak to about 24 percent and then stalled — and this hour examines who is missing school, why, what five million lost instructional hours cost, and the Maine responses with results behind them, from the Maine Engagement and Attendance Center and early warning systems to Maine Indian Education's drop from the fifties to 19.6 percent.
Sources: Maine Department of Education, Data Warehouse — Chronic Absenteeism (definition: enrolled at least 10 days, missed 10% or more of days enrolled, excused or unexcused) and Enrollment: https://www.maine.gov/doe/data-reporting/reporting/warehouse/visualizations Maine Department of Education, Maine's Model of School Support (chronic absenteeism as an accountability indicator): https://www.maine.gov/doe/Testing_Accountability/model Maine Engagement and Attendance Center (MEAC, established 2024; national Attendance Works figures cited there: 28% national rate in 2022-23, 30% peak, 16% in 2018-19; Maine 31% in 2021-22, 27% in 2022-23, 24% in 2023-24): https://www11.maine.gov/doe/index.php/meac Maine KIDS COUNT Data Center, Chronic Absenteeism (24.4% in 2024-25; 40,980 students; economically disadvantaged 34.5% vs 15.7% for higher-income students): https://datacenter.aecf.org/data/tables/10836-chronic-absenteeism?loc=21&loct=2 Maine Education Association, How Count ME In! is Tackling Chronic Absenteeism Across Maine (24.1% / nearly 41,000 students in 2023-24; peak 31.1% / 53,265 in 2021-22; 16.5% in 2017-18; 5,000,000 instructional hours lost in 2023-24; Jess Anderson quote; teacher-call timing at 1-3 and 4-6 days): https://maineea.org/maineeducatoronline/how-count-me-in-is-tackling-chronic-absenteeism-across-maine/ Count ME In!, For Families (barriers: transportation, work schedules, caregiving, housing, long distances, weather, rural access; support-focused documentation steps): https://www.countmeinmaine.org/for-families Maine DOE Newsroom, Maine Engagement and Attendance Center Continues Bringing Statewide Partners Together (June 17 meeting; MEAC partners Count ME In! and Maine PBIS; proactive root-cause mission): https://mainedoenews.net/2026/09/04/maine-engagement-and-attendance-center-continues-bringing-statewide-partners-together-to-strengthen-student-attendance/ Bureau of Indian Education, Maine Indian Education Posts Landmark Gains in Attendance and Achievement (systemwide 19.6% in 2024-25; Indian Island School 13.1%; Sipayik Elementary 18.7%; Indian Township School 27.0%; Maine statewide ~24%): https://www.bie.edu/news-article/maine-indian-education-posts-landmark-gains-attendance-and-achievement-superintendent Maine Department of Education, BARR 2026 State Handout (92 BARR schools, 11,250 students, 2,667 educators, vs 463 non-BARR schools; chronic absenteeism decline 14.6 points in BARR schools): https://www.maine.gov/doe/sites/maine.gov.doe/files/inline-files/BARR%20-%202026%20State%20Hadnout%20-%207.22.2026.pdf University of Southern Maine, Maine Education Policy Research Institute, 2026 report for policymakers (enrollment roughly 4% below pre-pandemic; chronic absenteeism 31% in 2021-22, 24% in 2023-24, 16% pre-pandemic): https://usm.maine.edu/cepare/wp-content/uploads/sites/481/2026/07/2026_June_MEPRI-Report_Implications-for-Policymakers_FINAL.pdf Brewer School Department, Chronic Absenteeism and Attendance Information (Maine compulsory attendance ages 7-17; absent if not present for more than 50% of the day; state reporting and truancy reporting to DHHS and law enforcement): https://www.breweredu.org/article/70421
Verification steps for items without a stable URL: For the Maine Engagement and Attendance Center Attendance Tracker results (28% average decline in chronically absent students and 32% decline in students failing one or more courses after two years), search maine.gov for "Maine Engagement and Attendance Center Year in Review" and open the Student Supports MEAC Year-in-Review PDF dated June 3, 2026. For the Portland Public Schools high school chronic absenteeism figure of about 42 percent, search the Citizen Portal Portland Public Schools (Maine) feed for the school board meeting summary dated September 22, 2026. For the rural school-based health centers study, search PubMed Central for "School-Based Health Centers and School Attendance in Rural Areas." For Maine's attendance coordinator requirements and highly-mobile-student guidance, search maine.gov for "Comprehensive Attendance Resource Guide" (Maine Department of Education PDF). For the Portland East End elementary school reduction from 25 percent to 13 percent, search Portland Press Herald coverage of Portland Public Schools chronic absenteeism at East End Community School. Section 504 and IDEA are discussed as federal law: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act.

item.title: [Massachusetts] Education Trends — The Enrollment Decline and the Chapter 70 Reckoning
item.description:
Massachusetts public school enrollment fell to 867,825 students in 2025-26, the lowest total since 1994, and this episode traces the birth, housing, and immigration forces behind the decline and the Chapter 70 funding reckoning it has forced.
Sources: - Commonwealth Beacon, Massachusetts public schools are entering an era of fewer students (enrollment 867,825 in 2025-26, birth data, Gateway City and rural analysis, Chapter 70 and Foundation Budget Review Commission reporting), via Reporter Today: https://www.reportertoday.com/eastprovidence/premium/stories/school-enrollment-decline-raises-big-education-economic-questions,56230 - Boston Globe reporting summarized by Country 102.5, Massachusetts Public School Enrollment Drops to Lowest Point in Three Decades (more than 15,000 students shed 2024 to 2025; Chelsea, Everett, Framingham, and Marlborough down more than 5 percent): https://country1025.com/2026/01/13/massachusetts-public-school-enrollment-drops-to-lowest-point-in-three-decades/ - Massachusetts Legislature, Legislature Finalizes Fiscal Year 2027 Budget (Chapter 70 aid of 7.66 billion dollars, 160 dollars per pupil minimum aid, Special Education Circuit Breaker at 654.6 million dollars, Foundation Budget Review Commission revived): https://malegislature.gov/PressRoom/Detail?pressReleaseId=1431 - Massachusetts Teachers Association, FY27 State Budget Highlights (rural school aid, English learner enrollment offset, circuit breaker detail): https://www.massteacher.org/resource-library/state-budget-news - Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, Massachusetts Releases 2026 MCAS Results (chronic absenteeism 17.1 percent in 2025-26, down from 22.2 percent in 2022-23): https://www.mass.gov/news/massachusetts-releases-2026-mcas-results-highlighting-areas-of-progress-and-new-supports-for-students - Needham Observer, Early headcount shows drop in kindergarten enrollment (Needham September counts, superintendent and McKibben Demographic Associates analysis): https://needhamobserver.com/early-headcount-shows-drop-in-kindergarten-enrollment/ - Neighborhood View, Malden School Committee enrollment and accountability report, October 2026: https://neighborhoodview.org/2026/10/12/school-committee-sees-enrollment-declines-academic-improvements-as-parents-raise-after-school-program-concerns/ - To verify any district enrollment figure: go to profiles.doe.mass.edu, search the district by name, open Enrollment Data, and compare the October 1 totals for 2015-16, 2024-25, and 2025-26. To verify Chapter 70 figures: search mass.gov for Chapter 70 FY27 district aid and open your district's summary.

item.title: [NH] NH Education Trends in Southern NH — October 23, 2026: HB 1817 and the Free Seat
item.description:
Alex and Jordan devote the full hour to House Bill 1817, the 2026 law giving resident Education Freedom Account students free seats in their district classes, clubs, teams, and career and technical programs while the state sends districts no funding for those seats, and trace what that means for Manchester, Nashua, Derry, Salem, and the southern New Hampshire corridor in its first fall.
Sources: - HB 1817 as adopted by both bodies, with fiscal note (NH Department of Education: likely significant cost at local, state, or both level; impact indeterminable; about $6,000 per career and technical seat): https://gc.nh.gov/bill_status/pdf.aspx?id=32821&q=billVersion - HB 1817 legislative history and votes (House 179-156, Senate 15-8, signed June 19, 2026, Chapter 183, effective August 18, 2026): https://legiscan.com/NH/bill/HB1817/2026 - NH Department of Education, Technical Assistance Advisory on HB 1817 (issued September 25, 2026; districts asked to review enrollment and fee policies): https://www.education.nh.gov/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/2026/ta-hb1817.pdf - NH Department of Education, Technical Advisory on access to public school curricular and cocurricular programs, RSA 193:1-c (home educated students in grades 7-12 counted in average daily membership for adequacy aid): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/technical-advisory-rsa193-1-c.pdf - Reaching Higher NH, Recapping the 2026 Legislative Session (HB 1817 summary, 50 percent enrollment cap, district cost warning): https://www.reachinghighernh.org/content-item/554/2026-legislative-recap - New Hampshire School Boards Association, 2026 Legislative Summary (resident-only scope, instructional time measurement unresolved): https://nhsba.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-NHSBA-LEG-SUMMARY-8.18.2026.pdf - NEA-NH, New Education Laws guide (HB 1817 access without the state support given for home education students): https://neanh.org/advocating-change/new-from-nea-nh/090526-nea-nh-legislative-update-new-education-laws-state-primary - Childrens Scholarship Fund New Hampshire, EFA program reaches 12,500-student enrollment cap for 2026-27 (13,443 eligible, 943 waitlisted): https://nh.scholarshipfund.org/new-hampshire-education-freedom-account-program-reaches-12500-student-enrollment-cap/ - RSA 194-F:2, Education Freedom Account program and qualifying expenses, including services contracted from a district public school: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-hampshire/title-xv/chapter-194-f/section-194-f-2/ - EdChoice, New Hampshire Education Freedom Account program stats (average account value about $4,795 in 2025-26, cap escalator): https://www.edchoice.org/school-choice/programs/education-freedom-account-program/ - NH Education Department Special Education Procedural Safeguards Handbook, December 2024 (parentally placed students, equitable services, services plans): https://files.smartsites.parentsquare.com/8931/nhed_special_education_procedural_safeguards_handbook_-_updated_december_2024.pdf - NH Career and Technical Education, Parents page (28 centers statewide; a two-year CTE program costs about $8,000 more than standard tuition): https://nh-cte.org/parents/ - NH School Scoop, October 13, 2026 (Manchester class size caps of 20, 25, and 24 for labs; HB 1817 summary): https://nhschoolscoop.substack.com/p/nh-school-scoop-october-13-2026
To verify items without a stable URL: (1) New Hampshire Bulletin, October 12, 2026 reporting on the September 25 advisory and district capacity, prerequisite, and tryout limits: search newhampshirebulletin.com for HB 1817 EFA public school classes October 2026. (2) Town and county EFA take-up rates (Manchester about 9 percent; Rockingham County 10 percent rising to 15 percent): search the New Hampshire Bulletin for education freedom accounts double low-income recipients, which reports the Department of Education town-level data. (3) Timberlane Regional High School CTE budget figures (about $270,000 tuition, about $156,289 transportation, 143 to 158 students) and the Londonderry CTE consultant figures (about 149 students, $2,000 to $3,000 per student): search citizenportal.ai for Timberlane Regional High School CTE budget and for Londonderry School District CTE consultant.

item.description:

item.title: The Children the State Can No Longer Count: New Hampshire's Home Education Freedom Act
item.description:
On July 1, 2026, New Hampshire's Home Education Freedom Act (HB 1268) took effect - repealing the homeschool notice, the required subjects, the portfolio, and the annual evaluation all at once, and ending the state's count of home educated children. What does a state owe a child it has decided not to see? A special report: the old law and the new law, section by section; the supporters' case in their own words; the Department of Education webpage still teaching a repealed statute; the EFA contrast - public money still carries paperwork, private choice now carries none; and how New Hampshire stacks up against Maine, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut.

Hawaii's official enrollment count for twenty twenty-six to twenty twenty-seven is one hundred sixty-one thousand one hundred two students, unevenly spread across complex areas, which sets up a year of redistricting before any consolidation study — plus a legislative proposal for dyslexia-sensitive reading screening in a state lawmakers say has no dyslexia-specific law.
Sources: - Hawaii State Department of Education, Official Enrollment Count SY 2026-27 (PDF) — state total 161,102 K-12 across 296 schools, 1,585 Pre-K, complex area and grade-level counts, charters 13,446 across 38 schools: https://hawaiipublicschools.org/wp-content/uploads/HIDOEenrollment2026-27.pdf - K-12 Dive, 'Hawaii to weigh redistricting before consolidating schools,' September 24, 2025 — enrollment 174,704 in 2020-21 to 163,651 in 2025-26; 2026-27 spent exploring and implementing redistricting; consolidation study after, potential transition as soon as July 2028: https://www.k12dive.com/news/hawaii-to-weigh-redistricting-before-consolidating-schools/760923/ - Hawaii State Legislature, House Bill 1891, Thirty-Third Legislature, 2026 (introduced text) — findings that Hawaii is the only state lacking dyslexia-specific laws, current K-9 universal screener limits, proposed dyslexia-sensitive linguistically appropriate screening beginning 2027-28 for kindergarten through grade 3 and first-time entrants, interventions through the Hawaii multi-tiered system of supports: https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/sessions/session2026/bills/HB1891_.HTM - Hawaii State Legislature, House Bill 1784, 2026 — findings on the five-year 60 million dollar federal literacy grant for evidence-based literacy practices including screener evaluation, following a nearly 50 million dollar grant in 2019; search data.capitol.hawaii.gov for 'HB1784 2026 dyslexia literacy'

item.title: The Right That Stops at the Schoolhouse Door
item.description:
Lock the door, pull the shade, move the children to the hard corner. The lockdown drill is rehearsed in every school in America — and it is the closest thing public school teachers have to a workplace safety law. In this national episode, Alex and Jordan trace why: a single definition in the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 wrote every public employee in the country out of the nation's workplace-safety law, and the right to a workplace free from recognized hazards stops at the schoolhouse door. We built the count from OSHA's own registry: in 29 of the 56 states, districts, and territories, a public school employee has a real safety regulator; in 27, there is no one to complain to. Plus the bargain police and firefighters got and teachers never did, the IDEA collision that stops abatement where a student is the hazard, New York's 2024 law that proves the fix can be built, and New Hampshire's paper right — a petition process aimed at a rulebook with no violence standard in it. The full written feature and the jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction coverage map are published with this story at educationacrossthestates.com.
Sources — OSHA, State Plans (22 full plans covering private and public sector workers; 7 public-sector-only plans: Connecticut, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, U.S. Virgin Islands): https://www.osha.gov/stateplans ; Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970, section 3(5) definition of "employer" and section 5(a)(1) General Duty Clause: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/completeoshact and https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/section5-duties ; Littler, "New York Amends Workplace Violence Prevention Law to Extend Coverage to Public Schools" (Labor Law section 27-b, effective January 4, 2024): https://www.littler.com/news-analysis/asap/new-york-amends-workplace-violence-prevention-law-extend-coverage-public-schools ; Parker & Covert LLP on California SB 553 / Labor Code section 6401.9 (written workplace violence prevention plans, including school districts, by July 1, 2024): https://www.parkercovert.com/new-requirements-for-california-employers-to-implement-workplace-violence-prevention-plans-by-july-2024 ; New Hampshire RSA chapter 277 (277:13-a employee petition for inspection; 277:15-a post-incident inspections naming school districts): https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XXIII/277/277-mrg.htm ; Individuals with Disabilities Education Act discipline provisions, 20 U.S.C. 1415(k): https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/20/1415 ; Bricker & Eckler on Ohio's Public Employment Risk Reduction Program (PERRP, ORC chapter 4167): https://www.brickergraydon.com/insights/publications/PERRP-are-your-employees-safe

item.title: [NH] Nashua School Board Watch — Correction: Finance & Operations Committee, October 19, 2026
item.description:
MINUTES CORRECTION: The formal minutes for the October 19, 2026 Finance & Operations Committee are now posted, and this watch checked them against our corrected report on that meeting, as promised. Most of the reporting is confirmed exactly — all seven special education contract approvals passed 2-0 at the caps we reported (ACM Staffing $79,560, which also resolves the packet discrepancy we flagged; Beyond Words $46,800; Champion Speech Therapy $90,935; SLP Mama-to-be amendment to $76,930; Amergis $43,680; BlazerWorks $206,640; special education services $57,000 — $554,645 in new or expanded authority), the FY27 September Transfer Report was approved, and the solar power purchase agreements for Main Dunstable, Birch Hill, Bicentennial, and the School Administration Building were approved. One money item was materially different: we reported three CERF vehicles totaling $223,523, including a $56,296 Transit van; the minutes record approval of four purchases totaling $266,777.07 — dump truck $90,100, F-250 pickup $77,127, Maverick pickup $34,407, and a field tractor $65,143.07, with no Transit van. The minutes also record an information item we missed: a proposed joint city-school ERP system at approximately $9 million (no vote taken). Only two committee members were present, and every vote passed 2-0.
Also in this episode: the Board of Education did not meet on Monday, October 26 as previously listed — the full board meets Wednesday, October 28 at 5:00 PM to take up these recommendations (with the dump truck and Maverick amounts already revised in that agenda), followed by the Facilities Master Plan public hearing at 6:00 PM. Official documents confirm a board meeting on November 16 but do not label it the facilities vote; that timing is unconfirmed.
Watch board meetings live via the meeting link on nashua.edu under the Board of Education section.
Listener poll: https://strawpoll.com/xVg718Km6yr
Sources: - Nashua School District, Finance & Operations Committee Minutes, October 19, 2026 (2-page PDF, linked from the Finance and Operations page on nashua.edu): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1B1fUfvntA1NU-zFrUNd1kSDfVvEZaOf3/view?usp=drive_link - Nashua School District, Finance and Operations agendas and minutes page (nashua.edu > Our District > Board of Education > BOE Meeting Agendas and Minutes > Finance and Operations): https://www.nashua.edu/our-district/board-of-education/boe-meeting-agendas-and-minutes/finance-and-operations - Nashua School District, Board of Education Meeting Agenda and Attachments, October 28, 2026 (164-page PDF, linked from the BOE Meeting Agendas and Minutes page): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1MmNdFQyC0MMlAfyvi-IxksfgvUNDZvUo/view?usp=drive_link - Nashua School District, BOE Meeting Agendas and Minutes, October 2026 section (October 13 and October 19 minutes posted; no October 26 entry): https://www.nashua.edu/our-district/board-of-education/boe-meeting-agendas-and-minutes - Nashua Board of Education meeting schedule, October-November 2026 (nashua.edu; October 26 blank, October 28 BOE meeting 5 PM + public hearing 6 PM, November 16 BOE meeting 6 PM): https://www.nashua.edu/our-district/board-of-education/boe-meeting-schedule - Verification steps: open nashua.edu, choose Our District > Board of Education > BOE Meeting Agendas and Minutes > Finance and Operations, open the October 19, 2026 Minutes PDF, and compare each recorded 2-0 vote and dollar amount against this episode; then open the October 28, 2026 Agenda and Attachments PDF (Finance & Operations recommendations, pp. 1-2) to see the amounts the full board will vote on.

item.title: [Colorado] Deep Dive — Four Schools, Not Nine: The Poudre Vote
item.description:
The Poudre School District board voted 5-2 at 1:56 in the morning on October 28, 2026 to close four schools — Blevins Middle School and Beattie, Johnson and Putnam elementary schools — consolidate Centennial and Poudre Community Academy, and redraw the Bacon Elementary boundary, all for 2027-28, while sparing the three mountain schools outright and delaying the Irish and Timnath closures a year with conditions. item.title: [Hawaii] Deep Dive — Known, Warned, Unprotected: The McKinley Case and the Duty to Protect a Student Who Could Not Consent
item.description:

Hayashi restored the full $14,167,354.81 judgment against the State after a 66-day trial found the Department of Education negligently failed to protect a McKinley High School special education student who could not consent — a full walk through the court's chronology of ignored warnings, the damages award line by line, the four holdings that reversed the 30 percent cut, and what school teams must do differently.

item.title: [Minnesota] Deep Dive — The Commission That Said No: Minnesota's $250 Million Special Education Cut
item.description:
The Blue Ribbon Commission was ordered to cut $250 million per biennium from Minnesota special education aid while maintaining FAPE — and unanimously told the Legislature not to do it. This deep dive walks through the charge, the enrollment and cross-subsidy numbers, each of the four savings recommendations in dollars (ADSIS, FIN 728 transportation, charter tuition aid, and Hold Harmless), the automatic default cut that follows if the Legislature does nothing, Saint Paul's $9 million-a-year exposure and its separate English learner vote due by October 30, Fridley's updated audit scrutiny, and the Permanent School Fund amendment on the November 3 ballot where a blank counts as a no.

item.title: [New York] Deep Dive — Four Students, $3.3 Million, and a School the State Never Approved
item.description:
New Rochelle spent at least $3,328,452.60 in tuition and transportation on four students at Shrub Oak International School — a private school the State Education Department said in writing was not state-approved, could not be recommended by a committee on special education, and had no state funding mechanism — and payments continued into 2023-24 after warnings in 2020, a hearing, and a State Review Officer decision. item.title: [Rhode Island] Deep Dive — The $525 Million Question: Rhode Island's Funding Formula Overhaul and the Students with Disabilities in the Middle

item.title: [Ohio] Deep Dive — The Bus Is Voluntary, the Ride Is a Right: Columbus, COTA, and the Students a Budget Vote Cannot Rewrite
item.description:

item.title: [Utah] Deep Dive — Over the One Percent Line: Utah's Alternate Assessment Cap
item.description:
Utah is over the federal one percent cap on alternate assessment participation for a second year in a row, fifty-three districts and charter schools owe the state justification letters in January, and the state cannot seek a waiver because overall test participation sits below ninety-five percent — a complete walkthrough of the cap, the waiver trap, the consequences other states have actually faced, Utah's own eligibility criteria, and what IEP teams, administrators, and parents should do before the spring testing window.
Sources: - Citizen Portal, 'Special education team warns Utah likely over ESSA 1% alternate-assessment cap; federal consequences possible' (October 26, 2026), reporting the USBE special education presentation: second year above 1%, 53 LEAs over 1% in at least one subject, January justification letters, waiver blocked by sub-95% participation, monitoring calls and potential Title I consequences: https://citizenportal.ai/articles/11481766/utah/utah-legislative-branch/utah-government-divisions/utah-state-board-of-education/special-education-team-warns-utah-likely-over-essa-1-alternate-assessment-cap-federal-consequences-possible - U.S. Department of Education, letter granting North Carolina's 1% cap waiver (2026), recording North Carolina's documented 95% participation: https://www.dpi.nc.gov/10-percent-participation-waiver-approval-letter/download?attachment - Hanshaw filings due this week.

item.title: [U.S. Virgin Islands] Deep Dive — The Wait Before the Clock Starts: Evaluations, Staffing, and Child Find
item.description:
The territory finished every consented initial evaluation on time in its latest federal report — seventy of seventy within forty-five days — yet federal reviewers could not validate its child find data, its own monitors cited both districts for the lapse between referral and consent, and its own Board of Education calls the special education vacancies a near civil rights violation: an hour on the unmeasured wait, the workforce underneath it, and the home-grown pipelines meant to end it.

item.title: [Utah] Education Daily — October 29, 2026: A Security Team for Every School
item.description:
Utah has launched Education Security Services, a roughly twenty-eight million dollar, four-year program that puts a dedicated K-12 cybersecurity team inside the Utah Cyber Center — and one hundred forty-seven of one hundred sixty-six eligible districts and charters have already enrolled. item.title: Special — "There Is No Teaching Without Learning": What Parents and Students Teach the IEP Team
item.description:
Paulo Freire wrote that whoever teaches learns in the act of teaching, and whoever learns teaches in the act of learning. In an IEP meeting, that sentence is either a description or an indictment. This special examines the IDEA's own design — parents as required IEP team members whose concerns the team must by law consider, students who must be invited and heard — the research on student-led IEPs and self-determination, and the practical difference between performing listening and actually learning from the family in the room. Produced by Charles Mayfield, Education Across the States.
Sources: - Paulo Freire, Pedagogy of Freedom: Ethics, Democracy, and Civic Courage (Rowman & Littlefield, 1998), Chapter 2, "There Is No Teaching Without Learning." - 20 U.S.C. 1414 (IDEA, IEP and evaluation provisions). - 34 CFR 300.321(a) (IEP Team membership, including parents); 34 CFR 300.321(b) (student invitation for transition services; preferences and interests considered if the student does not attend). - 34 CFR 300.322 (parent participation; notice and mutually agreed time and place); 34 CFR 300.501(b) (parent opportunity to participate in meetings on identification, evaluation, placement, and FAPE). - 34 CFR 300.324(a)(1)(ii) (team must consider the concerns of the parents for enhancing the education of their child); 34 CFR 300.320(a)(1) (present levels); 34 CFR 300.304(b) and 300.305(a) (evaluations and reevaluation reviews draw on information provided by the parents). Regulations text: ecfr.gov, Title 34, Part 300. - Martin, J.E., Van Dycke, J.L., Christensen, W.R., Greene, B.A., Gardner, J.E., & Lovett, D.L. Five bills introduced October 29, 2026 would publish special education complaint investigation reports, add independent investigators for complaints against the state department itself, assign compensatory-services decisions, and enforce corrective plans — plus a Senate-passed bill guaranteeing county college admission offers to graduates. Sources: NJ21st, 'Five bills could change New Jersey's special education complaint process,' October 30, 2026, https://nj21st.com/2026/10/30/five-bills-could-change-new-jerseys-special-education-complaint-process/ (bill texts: search each bill number — A5717, A5718, A5719, A5720, A5721, S4931, S4929, S4926, S4927, S4928 — in the New Jersey Legislature bill search at njleg.state.nj.us); N.J.A.C. 6A:14-9.2, Complaint investigation (current process: search '6A:14-9.2 complaint investigation' on nj.gov, New Jersey Department of Education, Office of Special Education); NJ21st, October 15, 2026 Hillside follow-up and this show's October 21, 2026 Hillside deep dive (NJDOE May 6, 2026 report, complaint C2026-7612); NJTODAY.NEWS, 'Senate OKs bill guaranteeing county college admission offers to graduates,' October 29, 2026, https://njtoday.news/2026/10/29/senate-oks-bill-guaranteeing-county-college-admission-offers-to-graduates/ (based on a New Jersey Senate Democrats press release on S-4128).

item.title: [South Carolina] Education Daily — October 30, 2026: The Questions Below the Candidates
item.description:
South Carolina has no statewide questions on the November 3, 2026 ballot — every school-money decision is local. A voter's guide to the three biggest: Dorchester County's proposed new one percent education sales tax for Districts Two and Four, Charleston County's vote to extend its existing tax through 2034, and Spartanburg District Two's two linked bond questions, plus this morning's Education Freedom Tax Credit Study Committee meeting and how to check your own sample ballot before early voting ends October 31.
Sources — Dorchester School District Two, Education Sales Tax Referendum page including Dorchester County Council Resolution 26-07 (adopted August 3, 2026) and the SC Revenue and Fiscal Affairs projection of 688.2 million dollars over 15 years: https://www.ddtwo.org/Nov3 ; Charleston County School District, November 2026 Education Sales Tax Referendum page: https://www.ccsdschools.com/about-us2/one-cent-sales-tax ; Spartanburg.com, District 2 Voters Face Two School Bond Questions November 3rd (October 29, 2026), summarizing the Spartanburg District Two referendum announcement and State Election Commission ballot wording; WCIV (ABC News 4 Charleston), Growth and aging campuses drive push for 1-cent sales tax vote in Dorchester County, for District Four's roughly 103 million dollar share and its stated construction shortfall — search mytvcharleston.com for that headline to verify; South Carolina Department of Education, Education Freedom Tax Credit Study Committee meeting notice (October 28, 2026) and published agenda at ed.sc.gov/newsroom/eftc-agenda — search ed.sc.gov news releases for Education Freedom Tax Credit Study Committee to verify; South Carolina Election Commission referendum listing and voter tools at scvotes.gov — search scvotes.gov for the November 3, 2026 referendum listing and sample ballot lookup to verify your own ballot.

item.title: [Iowa] Education Daily — November 2, 2026: Sixty Percent Is the Whole Game
item.description:
Election eve in Iowa is decided by one number: sixty percent. Hinton's majority-yes bond that still lost last year, its smaller fourth attempt, Norwalk's bus facility timeline reported this morning, Kirkwood's eighty-eight million dollar ask, and Lone Tree's geothermal question — all shaped by the supermajority every Iowa school bond must clear tomorrow.
Sources: - KNIA-KRLS (Nov 2, 2026), Norwalk Transportation Facility Among Projects in Proposed Bond — transportation facility 10 to 11 million dollars, city lease ends 2029, land purchased, bids expected December or January, construction spring 2027, elementary school 42 million dollars, together about 90 percent of the 65 million dollar bond: https://www.kniakrls.com/norwalk-transportation-facility-among-projects-in-proposed-bond/ - Norwalk Community School District, Norwalk School Board Approves Petition for November 3rd Bond Referendum — 65 million dollars, no property tax rate increase, debt service levy held at 4.05 dollars per 1,000 dollars since 2013, 42.5 million dollar 750-student elementary school, 314 petition signatures vs 222 required: https://www.norwalkschools.org/news/2026/08/norwalk-school-board-approves-petition-for-november-3-bond-referendum/ - Hinton Community School District, Bond 2026 (district site, checked Nov 2, 2026) — 8.6 million dollars, middle/high school only, elementary addition removed, 13-year repayment saving about 2.2 million dollars in interest, SAVE funding reduction from 2027, borrowing limit about 20 million dollars vs at least 60 million for a new school: https://sites.google.com/hintonschool.com/bond26/home - Hinton Community School District, Bond 2025 results (district site) — November 4, 2025 referendum rejected, 460 yes (58.75 percent) to 323 no, below Iowa's 60 percent threshold: https://sites.google.com/hintonschool.com/bond25/home - KLEM 1410 (Oct 20, 2026), Hinton CSD Superintendent speaks on fourth attempt of bond vote — fourth consecutive annual attempt, 60 percent required, prior feedback on ballot wording and tax impact: https://klem1410.com/2026/10/20/hinton-csd-superintendent-speaks-on-fourth-attempt-of-bond-vote/ - The Gazette via Hometown Current, What voters should know about Kirkwood's 88 million dollar bond measure — five investment areas, estimated 9.35 dollars per year per 100,000 dollars assessed value, 41,000 learners, polls November 3 from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., in-person absentee voting through November 2, election-day registration: https://www.hometowncurrent.com/news/what-voters-should-know-about-kirkwood-s-88-million-bond-measure/article_7a75d9c9-92ae-4491-ae52-a455cd8f37b7.html - Lone Tree Community School District, 2026 Bond Referendum — 6.9 million dollar geothermal heating and cooling replacement, property tax rate unchanged, ballot language: https://www.lonetreecsd.org/district/2026_bond_referendum - Iowa Department of Education, State Board September 17, 2026 Chapter 17 notice of intended action (ARC 0653D) — open enrollment denial reporting hearing November 3, 2026, 8 to 9 a.m., comments due 4:30 p.m. November 3, 2026: search educate.iowa.gov for the September 17, 2026 State Board Chapter 17 rules item.

item.title: What Remains Unanswered: The Tax-Cap Vote, and Nashua's Facilities Decision
item.description:
Tomorrow, every New Hampshire voter decides Question Two — and the honest headline is how much remains unanswered: a ballot sentence still in dispute, an inflation term the question never defines, and no official district-by-district accounting of what the school tax cap would cost. item.title: [NH] Nashua School Board Watch — Board of Education Meeting, October 28, 2026: Vehicles Approved 8-0 and $601,545 in Special Education Contracts Pass
item.description:
The full Nashua Board of Education met Wednesday, October 28, 2026 and approved the Finance & Operations recommendations: four CERF vehicle purchases totaling $271,610.07 (one-ton dump truck $92,735; F-250 pickup $77,127; Maverick pickup $36,605; field tractor $65,143.07) on the night's only counted vote, 8-0; solar power purchase agreements for Main Dunstable, Birch Hill, Bicentennial, and the School Administration Building, with final contracts returning to the board before any end-of-year signing; seven special education service agreements with caps totaling $601,545 (ACM Staffing $79,560; Beyond Words $46,800; Champion Speech Therapy $90,935; SLP Mama-to-be amendment to $76,930; Amergis $43,680; BlazerWorks $206,640; special education services $57,000), each passed on a voice vote with no count stated; and the FY27 September transfer of $304,407 from wages to contracted services. The board also heard 2025-2026 state assessment results (Nashua proficiency 45% ELA, 34% math, 27% science). Two printed agenda items did not happen: the consent agenda was never taken up in the recording, and the five special education policy first readings (ACE, IHBA, IHBA-R1, IHBAA, IHBAB) previewed from the agenda were not given a first reading — no second-reading date was set. The separate 6 PM Facilities Master Plan public hearing that followed drew roughly 80 speakers, overwhelmingly urging the board to close no schools; no vote was taken, and the board deliberates November 16 (whether it votes that night is unconfirmed). Formal minutes for October 28 are not yet posted; this episode is based on the meeting recording and packet, and this watch will verify it against the minutes when they post.
Watch board meetings live via the meeting link on nashua.edu under the Board of Education section.
Listener poll: https://strawpoll.com/xVg718Km6yr

item.title: Understanding School Evaluations — KBIT-2: What the Test Measures, Reading Results and Building IEPs
item.description:
A special extra episode of Understanding School Evaluations on the KBIT-2 (Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test, Second Edition): what its three subtests — Verbal Knowledge, Riddles, and Matrices — actually measure, how to read the Verbal, Nonverbal, and IQ Composite scores with their confidence bands, and why a 20-minute brief test must never carry an eligibility, intellectual-disability, or gifted decision alone. Includes the edition update (the KBIT-2 Revised, published August 2022 with 2021 norms, is the current edition), the language supports for multilingual students, the re-evaluation and universal-screening uses, the full pitfalls list, the 60-second explanation every parent should hear, and the Kaufman family connection to the KABC-II NU. The scheduled series continues Monday with DAS-II Part A. Sources: Pearson, Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test | Second Edition (KBIT-2) product page (Kaufman & Kaufman, 2004; ages 4:0-90:0; Qualification Level B; approximately 20 minutes; Crystallized/Fluid/IQ Composite standard scores, M=100, SD=15; conormed with KTEA-II Brief Form): https://www.pearsonassessments.com/store/en/usd/p/100000390.html ; Pearson, Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test, Second Edition Revised (KBIT-2 Revised) product page (publication date August 2022; 2021 norms; manual and Q-global scoring; Nonverbal subtest administrable in any language, Spanish instructions/teaching in the stimulus book; Verbal subtests in English with credit for correct responses in any language): https://www.pearsonassessments.com/store/en/usd/p/P100013000.html ; Pearson, KBIT-2 Revised comparison (2004 norms data collected 2002-2003; subtests unchanged with minimal item refreshing; scaled scores and scaled-score comparison for the verbal subtests; 90% and 95% confidence intervals; validity studies including WISC-V, WIAT-4, PPVT-5/EVT-3, CELF Preschool-3, Raven's 2; special-group studies in intellectual disability and gifted; KBIT-2 Revised verbal subtests substitutable into a KABC-II NU battery): https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/kbit/kbit2-revised-comparison.pdf ; Kaufman & Kaufman (2004), KBIT-2 manual psychometrics as cited in Mervis et al. (2012), Longitudinal assessment of intellectual abilities of children with Williams syndrome, American Journal on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (standardization sample of 2,120 examinees ages 4-90 stratified to U.S. Census; internal consistency coefficients .89-.96; KBIT-2 IQ correlation with WAIS-III Full Scale IQ r=.89): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3334347/ ; Bain & Jaspers (2010), Test review: Kaufman Brief Intelligence Test, Second Edition, Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment (manual mean test-retest coefficients: Verbal .91, Nonverbal .83, IQ Composite .90); 34 CFR 300.304, Evaluation procedures (variety of assessment tools; no single measure or assessment as the sole criterion; technically sound instruments; administration in the child's native language): https://ecfr.io/Title-34/Section-300.304 ; Guide to the NH Standards for the Education of Children with Disabilities (Ed 1100; Ed 1107.02 pattern of strengths and weaknesses; Ed 1109 evaluation procedures), Parent Information Center / NH Department of Education: https://picnh.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Guide-to-the-NH-Standards-9.01.2024.pdf . item.title: [New York] Deep Dive — Forty Students, One Hundred Twelve Students, and the Word That Decides Who Gets a Hearing
item.description:
New York City has formally proposed closing two Harlem schools — SEED Harlem, with forty students, half of them students with disabilities, and the Urban Assembly School for Global Commerce, with one hundred twelve — and relocating the Center School, with a Panel for Educational Policy vote on December 16, 2026; this deep dive covers each school's profile and demographics, fact-checks the enrollment rationale against the City Comptroller's October 29 report, explains the impact-statement and hearing rights city families hold under Education Law 2590-h, contrasts Buffalo, where Education Law 402-a makes those same steps optional, and lays out what a closure does and does not change in a student's IEP, plus a follow-up desk closing the SUNY fee-waiver item, reporting the continuing NYSED silence on the fifteen Shrub Oak questions at the November 4 check, and previewing today's Second Circuit mascot-ban arguments.
Sources: - Chalkbeat New York, NYC proposes closing 2 Harlem public schools, relocating Center School (Nov 2, 2026): https://www.chalkbeat.org/newyork/2026/11/02/nyc-harlem-school-closures-center-school-relocation-mamdani/ - Chalkbeat New York, Mamdani faces tough choices on closures and mergers amid NYC enrollment drops, small-schools series part 3 (Oct 30, 2026): https://www.chalkbeat.org/newyork/2026/10/30/nyc-mamdani-samuels-plan-for-small-schools-crisis-mergers-closures/ - NYC Comptroller, Comptroller Levine Releases New Report Showing Scale of NYC's Declining Public School Population (Oct 29, 2026): https://comptroller.nyc.gov/newsroom/comptroller-levine-releases-new-report-showing-scale-of-nycs-declining-public-school-population/ - NYC Public Schools, December 16, 2026 — School Utilization Proposals (hearing dates Dec 1, 2, 3; comments through Dec 15, 6 PM): https://www.schools.nyc.gov/get-involved/families/panel-for-education-policy/2026-2027-pages/december-16-2026-school-utilization-proposals - The Standard, NY School Closing Law Is Optional Outside NYC. item.title: [Massachusetts] Deep Dive — The Morning After: A Second Term, Nine Questions, and Four School Votes Still Being Counted
item.description:
Governor Healey wins a second term and six of nine statewide questions are called — two still too close, including the state revenue cap — while the verified counts for Reading's override and the Swansea, Needham, and Hingham school building votes were still being posted on the morning of November 4, 2026, so this deep dive covers each vote's full stakes, the Proposition 2.5 and MSBA machinery underneath them, tonight's Boston School Committee hearing on closing Charlestown High, and the November calendar that decides what happens next.

item.title: [Montana] Deep Dive — Fifty-Five Votes in Terry: The Accessible Restroom, the Sinking Gym Floor, and Montana's Facilities Bill
item.description:
Fifty-five votes in Prairie County approved Terry's $1.5 million school bond on November 3, 2026 — a sewer main, a gym floor that can no longer be sanded, bleachers with wheelchair spaces, 1953 elementary windows, and the single-stall ADA restroom a building was missing, in a district whose superintendent said on the record that guests with mobility needs could not be accommodated. Plus the statewide facilities gap behind it, the still-missing YouthVote results, and the November-December Montana calendar.

item.title: [Nebraska] Education Daily — November 4, 2026: What the Ballot Did Not Decide
item.description:
Nebraska voters decided a constitutional amendment and at least two school bonds on November 3, but teacher pay was never on the ballot — today we trace the 0,000 minimum-salary petition that did not reach voters, the LB1182 bill that carries the same idea, and the Teacher Vacancy Survey that closes today with special education still the state's largest shortage.

item.title: [American Samoa] Deep Dive — Ninety-Nine Percent Graduate: What the Territory's Own Numbers Say About Proficiency, Reporting, and FAPE
item.description:

item.title: [New Hampshire] Special — Yes in Every Ward: Nashua Voted to Cap School Taxes and Still Couldn't
item.description:
On November 3, 2026, Nashua voters said yes to a school tax cap in all nine wards — 17,622 yes to 12,454 no — and the cap failed anyway, 424 votes short of the 60% threshold New Hampshire law requires. With no cap, the district's costs keep climbing toward a fiscal cliff, and its chosen answer is closing school buildings, with a facilities vote set for November 16. This special reads the other ledger: Nashua's own budget book. The central office (SAU 42) is proposed at 4,567,339 dollars for fiscal 2027 — 2.2% of the total budget, well under the 6% figure in the failed ballot question — but four administrative areas grew by about 1 million dollars in a single year (curriculum supervision +50.4%, special education administration +37.7%, staff services +37.6%, administrative offices +26.9%) in the same budget that eliminated 56 positions, 21 of them teachers. Holding those four lines flat would recover roughly three-fifths of what closing one elementary school saves. Every figure is from the documents listed below.
Sources: City of Nashua official election results, November 3, 2026: https://www.nashuanh.gov/202/Election-Results Nashua Ward 7 sample ballot (Question 2 text, RSA 32:5-i): https://www.nashuaindependent.com/content/files/2026/11/NASHUA-WARD-7-sample-ballot.pdf Nashua School District FY27 Budget Notebook (preliminary budget detail and personnel detail, February 17, 2026): https://nashuaedu.finalsite.com/our-district/board-of-education/nsd-operating-budget/fy27-budget-notebook Nashua School District FY2027 budget presentation to the Board of Aldermen, May 5, 2026, and FY2026 budget presentation, March 31, 2025 (district budget publications) NH Department of Education, Cost Per Pupil by District, 2024-25: http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/cost-per-pupil-fy2025.pdf Nashua Ink Link, October 17, 2026 (adequacy aid): https://nashua.inklink.news/cut-in-state-adequacy-aid-will-leave-nashua-school-district-trying-to-get-blood-from-a-stone-board-president-says/ Nashua Ink Link, October 22, 2026 (Harriman facilities options): https://nashua.inklink.news/harriman-presents-updated-facilities-master-plan-with-a-new-option/ Nashua Ink Link, June 24, 2026 (FY27 budget adoption): https://nashua.inklink.news/aldermen-pass-fiscal-year-2027-budget-with-amendments/ Nashua Ink Link, April 2026 (Special Education Trust Fund): https://nashua.inklink.news/special-education-trust-fund-depleted-in-less-than-6-months-for-contract-services-district-presents-plan-for-reconfiguration/

item.title: [NH] NH Education Deep Dive — A Dollar a Thousand: The Education Tax New Hampshire Never Cut
item.description:
In October 2021, Mark Manganiello, administrator of the NH Department of Education's Office of School Finance, explained the Statewide Education Property Tax (SWEPT) in a public webinar and previewed how it would change in 2023: the rate would fall to $1.00 per $1,000, the state would backfill about $211 million from the general fund on an ongoing basis, and the roughly 30 "excess SWEPT" communities would lose the right to keep their surplus. Five years later, this Deep Dive grades those predictions against the record. The rate is $1.03 per $1,000 for FY2027 — but not because the tax was cut. The levy is still the same $363 million dollar target RSA 76:3 has set since 2005; the rate fell because property values rose. The enacted 2023 change was a one-year reduction to $263 million that quietly expired. Excess SWEPT was never repealed — about 40 municipalities retain roughly $28.2 million in SFY 2027 — and in Rand v. State (June 10, 2025) the NH Supreme Court upheld retention as constitutional. Three weeks later, in ConVal (July 1, 2025), the same court held the state's $4,100 base adequacy amount facially unconstitutional and affirmed $7,356.01 per pupil as a conservative minimum threshold; the base is $4,351 in FY2027 and the legislature has not funded to the threshold, answering instead with HB 1815 (2026), which recasts adequacy as a state-local "shared responsibility" while its fiscal note states it does not change grant amounts. With property taxes supplying about $3.0 billion (72%) of the $4.2 billion in district revenue, the episode closes where the pressure lands: the November 3, 2026 Question 2 tax-cap votes, adopted in 78 districts and rejected in 64 in our verified tally, with Nashua voting 58.59% yes and still falling 424 votes short.
Sources: - NH Department of Education, "FY 2026 Adequate Education Aid" and "FY 2027 Adequate Education Aid" (adequacy grant explanations), education.nh.gov - NH Department of Revenue Administration, Fiscal Note Quick Guide on HB 769 (2025), revenue.nh.gov - NH Office of Legislative Budget Assistant, "House Ways and Means and Governor General Fund and Education Trust Fund Estimates," February 14, 2025, gc.nh.gov/lba - Rand v. State, 2025 N.H. 27 (N.H. June 10, 2025) - Contoocook Valley School District v. State, 2025 N.H. 29 (N.H. July 1, 2025) - NH Fiscal Policy Institute, "Why State Adequate Education Aid Varies by Community," October 2026, nhfpi.org - NH Fiscal Policy Institute, "Statewide Education Property Tax Change Provides Less Targeted Relief," 2021 (updated 2022), nhfpi.org - NH School Funding Fairness Project, "What is SWEPT?" and ConVal/Rand case summaries, fairfundingnh.org - NH Business Review, "NH Supreme Court rules wealthy municipalities can keep excess education property tax," June 10, 2025, nhbr.com - HB 1815 (2026), Chapter 19, NH General Court; HB 669, HB 739, HB 769 (2025) and HB 1708 (2026), NH General Court bill dockets - Reaching Higher NH, "Webinar: Understanding the Statewide Education Property Tax (SWEPT)," NH Education Network, October 2021 (statements by Mark Manganiello, NH Department of Education)

item.title: The Three-Year Plan, Part 1: The Review
item.description:
Part 1 of 5 — The Review. Glenbrook High School District 225, a high-performing district serving Glenview and Northbrook, Illinois, kept adding special education staff for years — and the achievement gap between students with and without IEPs stayed put. So the district did something harder than spending: it audited the whole system. Alex and Jordan open the public record on the Special Education Opportunity Review — what the Glenbrook board approved on February 10, 2025, what it cost ($110,000 in federal IDEA funds), what a systemic review examines that a budget cannot show, and the national backdrop: 7.5 million students now served under IDEA, 15 percent of public school enrollment. For parents, educators, administrators, and board members, this series separates the district's own board documents from the vendor's published account throughout, so listeners can weigh each claim by its source.
Sources: Glenbrook High School District 225, Board of Education memorandum, "Contracts Greater than $35,000" (Dr. R.J. item.title: The Three-Year Plan, Part 2: The Diagnostic
item.description:
Part 2 of 5 — The Diagnostic. How do you find out what a special education program actually is, as opposed to what the organizational chart says? Alex and Jordan walk through the method behind Glenbrook District 225's Special Education Opportunity Review: interviews and focus groups running from the superintendent to instructional assistants, a Guiding Coalition of district and school leaders, and the quantitative core — 207 special education staff across seven roles invited to share one full week of their schedules, with 88 percent participating, analyzed alongside achievement, staffing, inclusion, and financial data. The result is the series' headline number: special education teachers' time spent working directly with students ranged from 8 percent to 81 percent of the week, averaging 42 percent. For parents, educators, administrators, and board members — budgets tell you what a district bought; schedules tell you what students got. Vendor-reported figures are identified as such throughout.
Sources: District Management Group, "Turning a Special Education Review into a Three-Year Action Plan: Aligning Roles, Data, and Time at Glenbrook High School District 225 (IL)" (vendor case study, including the findings graphic and Exhibit 1, "Percent of Special Education Teacher Time Spent with Students," Schedule Sharing Data 2025), https://www.dmgroupk12.com/success-stories/glenbrook-high-school-district-225-il ; Glenbrook High School District 225, Board of Education memorandum, "Contracts Greater than $35,000" (February 10, 2025), https://glenbrook225.community.diligentoneplatform.com/document/c2f4dbf8-9346-4002-8472-1960acedde3c/

item.title: The Three-Year Plan, Part 3: The Finding
item.description:
Part 3 of 5 — The Finding. The review of Glenbrook District 225 produced three findings: administrative roles that had multiplied without becoming clear; case management and IEP service delivery that differed from building to building; and student data fragmented across four systems. Alex and Jordan take the findings one at a time, then go deep on the one Superintendent Dr. R.J. Gravel put at the center of the district's response — case management. Federal law never defines the case manager's job, yet everything in special education runs through that desk: Illinois's 14-school-day evaluation decision and 60-school-day consent-to-eligibility clocks, the federal annual review and three-year reevaluation cycle, prior written notice, service verification, and the compensatory-education exposure when services are missed. For parents, educators, administrators, and board members: consistency of system, individuality of service — the law promises both, and case management is where a district keeps or breaks that promise.
Sources: District Management Group, "Turning a Special Education Review into a Three-Year Action Plan" (vendor case study and findings graphic; Superintendent Gravel quotation as published by DMG), https://www.dmgroupk12.com/success-stories/glenbrook-high-school-district-225-il ; 23 Illinois Administrative Code 226.110 (14 school days to decide whether an evaluation is warranted; 60 school days from parental consent to eligibility determination and IEP meeting; initial IEP within 30 calendar days), as quoted in the Illinois SPED Collaborative FAQ (gac.illinois.gov) ; 34 CFR 300.303, 300.324, 300.503 (reevaluation at least every three years; annual IEP review; prior written notice)

item.title: The Three-Year Plan, Part 4: The Plan
item.description:
Part 4 of 5 — The Plan. Reviews are easy to shelve. Glenbrook District 225 handed its findings to the people who would have to live with the response: district leaders and more than 20 staff volunteers — teachers, psychologists, speech-language pathologists, and social workers — who wrote the district's own three-year plan. Alex and Jordan lay out the architecture: six workstreams (roles and responsibilities; resource model and case management; data and documentation; the academic and related services continuum; professional learning; communication), four guiding principles (students' needs first; clarity before change; protect what is working; reduce workload burdens), and a sequencing decision — all six workstreams start in year one, at different intensities, with staff committees setting their own goals. Plus the district's own parallel move: the January 2026 decision, driven by case-manager feedback, to replace its IEP software — what it cost, how it was phased, and why this series does not credit it to the review. For parents, educators, administrators, and board members.

item.title: The Three-Year Plan, Part 5: Making It Stick
item.description:
Part 5 of 5 — Making It Stick. Plans die of initiative fatigue, leadership turnover, and silence. Alex and Jordan close the series on accountability: Glenbrook District 225's three-year special education plan was born in public documents — an open board vote, a published price, federal money — so its follow-through can be audited from outside, by the parents, educators, administrators, and board members this show serves. What to ask any district: Where are the workstream goals posted? When does progress get reported to the board in public? And will the district ever count staff time again, to test whether the 8-percent-to-81-percent spread has narrowed? Plus the national frame that makes the lesson universal: 7.5 million students under IDEA, a federal contribution authorized at up to 40 percent of average per-pupil spending that has never reached even half that benchmark — and the five moves any district can copy from Glenbrook without hiring anybody.

item.title: [New Jersey] District Deep Dive — Jersey City Public Schools

item.title: [Oklahoma] District Deep Dive — Edmond Public Schools
item.description:
Edmond Public Schools is one of Oklahoma's strongest districts on test scores, ACT results, and voter support — and it has lost 1,523 students in two years and projects a $9.9 million deficit, with its finance chief giving the district about a year to a year and a half to find solutions. Alex and Jordan walk the full public record: academics and the graduation-rate accounting fight, the budget and the fund-balance clock, two passed bonds totaling $287 million and a new elementary school opening into a decline, the special-education staffing shortage, the unanimous 2024 Oklahoma Supreme Court library-books win, the flag controversy, a new superintendent and strategic plan, a reported administrator restructuring, and a school-by-school walk of all three high schools, six middle schools plus Horizon under construction, and twenty elementary schools — plus the still-unpublished outcome of the Statewide Charter School Board's November 5, 2026 special meeting.

item.title: [Ohio] District Deep Dive — Cleveland Metropolitan School District
item.description:
An honest good, bad, and ugly deep dive into the Cleveland Metropolitan School District: a record 83.1 percent graduation rate and proficiency gains in every tested subject, alongside a 2.5-star state report card, 54.2 percent chronic absenteeism, a 29-school Building Brighter Futures consolidation, 410 layoffs, a state performance audit, the Glenville football playoff court case, and the end of the Flock camera contract.

item.title: [Vermont] Education Trends — Enrollment Decline: From 98,000 Students to 73,000, Part One
item.description:
Vermont has lost more than a quarter of its public school students in two decades, from about 98,000 in fiscal 2005 to 73,000 in 2025, and Part One establishes the numbers district by district, the causes in evidence order (births, housing, newcomers), why fewer students cost more per student, and what shrinking enrollment does inside schools, plus the follow-ups due November 6, 2026.
Sources: - Seven Days, Feb 18, 2026, 'Vermont's School Enrollment Is Dropping at an Alarming Rate' (AOE long-run counts, Mount Abraham, Burlington, Washington Central, housing, Colchester): https://www.sevendaysvt.com/news/gen-zero/vermont-is-losing-school-age-kids-at-an-alarming-rate/ - Education Resource Strategies, Fall 2026, 'Enrollment Decline in New England' (NCES Common Core of Data 2018-19 to 2024-25; Vermont 87,074 to 81,398; largest-district table; causes; small-school costs): https://www.erstrategies.org/tap/enrollment-decline-new-england/ - Vermont Joint Fiscal Office, Apr 7, 2026, 'Vermont Education Finance — Cost Analysis' (FY26 LTWADM 142,564; per weighted pupil range $10,846.46–$19,089.92; student-to-staff ratio 4.4, lowest in nation, NCES fall 2022): https://legislature.vermont.gov/Documents/2026/Workgroups/Senate%20Education/Acts%20and%20Previous%20Major%20Legislation/Act%2073%20of%202025/W~Julia%20Richter~Vermont%20Education%20Finance%20Cost%20Analysis~4-7-2026.pdf - Seven Days, Oct 28, 2026, 'Vermont School Districts Already Face Tough Budget Decisions' (Act 169 threshold; Harwood, Hartford, Champlain Valley): https://www.sevendaysvt.com/news/education-news/vermont-school-districts-already-face-tough-budget-decisions/ - Waterbury Roundabout, Nov 3, 2026, on the Central Vermont Career Center Nov 5 combined count (18 towns, Barre Auditorium, clerk Tina Lunt): https://www.waterburyroundabout.org/education/career-center-election-results-to-be-tallied-on-thursday-nov-5 - Act 170 (H.955) Act Summary, Vermont Office of Legislative Counsel: https://legislature.vermont.gov/Documents/2026/Docs/ACTS/ACT170/ACT170%20Act%20Summary.pdf - To verify the AOE merger-committee profiles and Stowe retreat materials (no public posting found at the Nov 6, 2026 check): search education.vermont.gov for 'Weekly Field Memo' and the Agency news listings, and search 'Agency of Education updated school and district profiles merger committees'.

item.title: [Maine] Education Trends — One in Five: Special Education Costs, Placements, and the Regional Bet

Sources: - MEPRI, Regionalized Special Education Administration and its Potential to Improve Services to Maine Students (June 2026): https://mepri.maine.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/RegionalSpecialEd_June2026.pdf - item.title: [Connecticut] Education Trends — The Special Education Funding Squeeze
item.description:
Connecticut now identifies 94,960 students for special education and spent $3.2 billion serving them in 2024-25, but its first dedicated funding formula, the SEED grant, is funded at $30 million against roughly $185 million needed, and the Excess Cost grant reimburses only part of the most expensive placements — this episode works through the data, the 2025 reforms, Meriden's in-district alternative, the February 2026 out-of-state oversight report, and the Blue Ribbon Commission report due January 15, 2027.
Sources: - Strengthening Special Education Funding (School and State Finance Project — SEED $30M vs ~$185M needed, 16.2% for FY 2027; Excess Cost 66.8% to 71.5% partial reimbursement; nearly $3.3B annual spending): https://schoolstatefinance.org/our-work/current-initiatives/sped-funding - 2025 Legislative Session: Changes to Special Education Funding (School and State Finance Project — Public Acts 25-168, 25-67, 25-93; Excess Cost appropriation $221,119,782; rate schedule by January 1, 2028): https://schoolstatefinance.org/hubfs/Reports/2025%20Legislative%20Session%20Changes%20to%20Special%20Education%20Funding.pdf - The Rising Cost of Special Education Is Straining School Budgets (Hartford Courant via Governing, July 30, 2026 — 79,058 students in 2020 to 94,960; item.title: [New Hampshire] Education Daily — What Remains Unanswered Before Nashua's Facilities Decision
item.description:
Ten days after Nashua's voters said yes to a school tax cap in every ward and missed the sixty percent bar by four hundred twenty-four votes, the decision that will shape the city's schools for a generation sits with its Board of Education. Ahead of the board's Monday, November 16 meeting, this follow-up inventories what the public record still does not answer: whether the board will actually vote that night, which of the surviving Harriman options (A, B, C, D, or F) it would choose, what the options cost at October's updated-but-unpublished figures, whether the consultants' estimated savings of $1.6–1.8 million per closed school survive the transportation and transition costs Harriman says have not yet been figured in, and where the special education programs and Title One preschool classrooms housed in buildings on the closure lists would go — a question families are scheduled to hear about at Special Education Advisory Council meetings on December 2 and 16, after the decision. NH Education Daily will report what the board does on November 16 in the November 17 episode; follow the show and subscribe at educationacrossthestates.com so it reaches you.
Sources: - City of Nashua official election returns, November 3, 2026 (Question 2: 17,622 yes / 12,454 no, 58.59%): nashuanh.gov → City Clerk → Elections; archived copy in the Education Across the States records (nashua-city-official-results-2026-11-03.pdf). - Nashua Ink Link, "Nashua school board sets Oct. 21 presentation, Nov. 16 vote on facilities plan": https://nashua.inklink.news/nashua-school-board-sets-oct-21-presentation-nov-16-vote-on-facilities-plan/ - Nashua Ink Link, "Harriman presents updated Facilities Master Plan with a new option" (Oct. 21, 2026 — Option F added, Option E eliminated, updated costs presented without published figures): https://nashua.inklink.news/harriman-presents-updated-facilities-master-plan-with-a-new-option/ - Nashua Ink Link, "School district Facilities Master Plan presented to the Board of Aldermen" (June 4, 2026 — option cost bands; Harriman's Lisa Sawin on transportation and transition costs not yet figured in): https://nashua.inklink.news/school-district-facilities-master-plan-presented-to-the-board-of-aldermen/ - Nashua Ink Link, "Cut in state adequacy aid will leave Nashua School District 'trying to get blood from a stone,' board president says" (aid figures per Board President Jennifer Bishop): https://nashua.inklink.news/cut-in-state-adequacy-aid-will-leave-nashua-school-district-trying-to-get-blood-from-a-stone-board-president-says/ - Nashua Board of Education meeting of October 28, 2026 — meeting recording and 164-page agenda packet (approvals: vehicles $271,610.07, special education contracts $601,545, solar PPAs with final-approval condition; five special education policies not taken up; Facilities Master Plan public hearing, incl. the chair's caution on a November 16 vote): nashua.edu → Board of Education → meeting link. item.title: [Pennsylvania] Education Daily — November 9, 2026: Five Parts Per Billion
item.description:
Pennsylvania raised the school drinking-water lead reporting threshold from any detectable amount to five parts per billion this summer, in a system where testing itself is optional — and an analysis of the Department of Education's own list finds only sixty-seven of five hundred districts have ever reported elevated lead. Plus the follow-up desk: still no published recaps for Pittsburgh's November fifth north region session or Bethlehem's November fourth through sixth listening sessions, Philadelphia's Policy Committee on November twelfth, and the State Board's November nineteenth cut-score vote.
Sources — Pennsylvania Department of Education, Lead in School Drinking Water page (Section 742.1; five parts per billion reporting, immediate action, and alternative water duties; list of schools reporting elevated lead levels, updated quarterly): https://www.pa.gov/agencies/education/programs-and-services/schools/school-construction-improvements-reconfigurations/school-construction-and-facilities-plancon/lead-in-school-drinking-water ; Spotlight PA, July 23, 2026, on the budget change inserted in the final forty-eight hours, the fifteen-to-zero-to-five guidance history, and Act 20 of 2026 (search Spotlight PA for Pennsylvania school lead reporting, July 2026; syndicated version at explorejeffersonpa.com, July 23, 2026) ; TapWaterData analysis of PDE's elevated-lead spreadsheet, downloaded August 9, 2026 (sixty-seven of five hundred districts, nine hundred ninety-nine readings, median twenty-six point six parts per billion, eighty-eight rows since May 2026): https://www.tapwaterdata.com/blog/testing/pennsylvania-school-lead-water-reporting ; The Allegheny Front, September 25, 2026, interview on Act 20 of 2026 and the five parts per billion standard: https://www.alleghenyfront.org/pennsylvania-lead-level-school-drinking-water/ ; Chalkbeat Philadelphia, November 5, 2026, updated November 6, on the proposed PSSA and Keystone cut scores and the November nineteenth State Board vote: https://www.chalkbeat.org/philadelphia/2026/11/05/pennsylvania-proposes-changing-math-and-reading-cut-scores/
