item.title: [Utah] Education Daily — November 9, 2026: May Become Effective Is Not Effective
item.description:

item.title: Houston ISD Special, Part 1: The Takeover That Failed Its Own Test
item.description:
Part 1 of a three-part Texas special. The Texas Education Agency has placed Houston ISD, a district the state itself runs, on a six-month special education action plan: a state review of 650 student records, repair of every noncompliant IEP, staff training, public town halls, and a parent advisory group, with state funding at risk. The takeover's own exit criteria require special education to operate in compliance with the law.
Sources - Houston Chronicle, Claire Partain, Nov 6, 2026: 'Exclusive: TEA orders HISD must fix special education program bugs or face more state sanctions,' based on TEA documents (paywalled; archived via TexEdNews, texednews.com, Nov 9, 2026 listing, and the author's Muck Rack page). Terms of the plan as summarized there: state review of 650 student records; if many are wrong, individual meetings with thousands of families by February; staff training; town halls; parent advisory group. - ABC13 (KTRK), Lileana Pearson, Nov 9-10, 2026: 'Texas Education Agency orders Houston ISD to fix special education program or risk losing funding,' abc13.com: six-month action plan; TEA required family meetings before changes; HISD said they were completed in August; TEA disagreed; HISD declined an interview, said it is working with the state and will share town hall details soon. - Texas Education Agency press release, June 2, 2025, tea.texas.gov ('TEA Announces Extension of Houston ISD Intervention'): Board of Managers installed June 1, 2023; intervention extended to June 1, 2027; the three exit criteria, including 'Special education operates in compliance with requirements.' - TEA Commissioner letter to HISD, May 30, 2025 (official TEA PDF, tea.texas.gov): as of that date the district had not yet met any of the three exit criteria. - KPRC 2, July 15, 2026, click2houston.com: 'Parents urge HISD to pause special education restructuring after TEA findings': HISD's Student Success Program; district figures of over 21,000 students in special education and about 5,000 in self-contained settings; HISD's placement-versus-location position.

item.title: [Guam] Education Daily — November 10, 2026: Guam Series Part One — Teacher Pay: The Raise Without the Money
item.description:

item.title: [NH] Nashua School Board Watch — Correction: Board of Education Meeting, October 28, 2026
item.description:
A correction special report. The formal minutes for the October 28, 2026 Nashua Board of Education meeting are now posted, and this watch checked every vote and dollar in its November 3 report against them. The Consent Agenda did pass 7-0 — the earlier report said it never happened, and that was wrong. The solar agreements, each special education contract, and the September transfer report are all recorded in the minutes as 8-0. The vehicle total of $271,610.07 and the special education contract caps totaling $601,545 are confirmed exactly. The facilities hearing minutes confirm no facilities vote was taken and list 27 speakers. This episode also reports what was before the Finance and Operations Committee on November 9, 2026 as packet recommendations only — no recording or minutes were posted as of November 10, so no committee votes are reported — and what is next on November 16. You can watch board meetings live via the meeting link on nashua.edu under the Board of Education section. Listener poll: https://strawpoll.com/xVg718Km6yr
Sources: - Nashua School District, Board of Education meeting schedule (November 2026 calendar; Nov 9 Finance & Operations 4:30 PM, Nov 16 BOE listed 7:00-8:30 PM): https://www.nashua.edu/our-district/board-of-education/boe-meeting-schedule - Nashua School District, BOE Meeting Agendas and Minutes (Oct 28, 2026 regular meeting minutes, 3 pp, and Special BOE Public Hearing minutes, 1 p): https://www.nashua.edu/our-district/board-of-education/boe-meeting-agendas-and-minutes - BOE Minutes 10-28-26 (Drive): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1crcXWguVcWudRdsD8MsLAfMHeauH2X1g/view - Special BOE Minutes 10-28-26, Facilities Public Hearing (Drive): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1l2_n-OOYQEsE-DLgnU24lcbKMVdeG9GF/view?usp=drive_link - Finance and Operations Agenda and Attachments 11-9-26, 23 pp (Drive): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mcXXETCL5wBRoysoPp319xqRrcXQ__ct/view - Finance and Operations committee page: https://www.nashua.edu/our-district/board-of-education/boe-meeting-agendas-and-minutes/finance-and-operations - Nashua BOE Meetings YouTube channel (checked Nov 10, 2026: newest posted recording is Oct 28, 2026; no Nov 9 Finance & Operations recording posted): https://www.youtube.com/@NashuaBOEmeetings/videos - Prior episode corrected: [NH] Nashua School Board Watch — Board of Education Meeting, October 28, 2026 (ep-9157a690-fe73-4d49-91e5-3f4d364730cc), script and recording compared line by line against the posted minutes - Verification steps: minutes votes and dollar amounts compared against the prior episode script; contract caps summed independently ($601,545); vehicle amounts summed independently ($271,610.07); Nov 9 packet read in full (23 pp) and treated as recommendations only, with no votes inferred

item.title: [District of Columbia] Education Daily — November 11, 2026: Twenty-One Schools Beat the Prediction

item.title: [Colorado] Deep Dive — The Placement That Has to Keep Being Decided: Facility Schools and the ECEA Hearing
item.description:
Tomorrow, Thursday, November twelfth, the Colorado State Board of Education opens its hearing on proposed changes to the Exceptional Children's Educational Act rules — and the heart of the package is the facility school, the most restrictive placement in Colorado special education. The draft would make a facility placement a decision that has to keep being decided: a home-district representative at every IEP meeting, a team review in the first ninety to one hundred twenty days that can adjust the placement itself, discharge protections, a residency ladder and a Commissioner dispute procedure, and new evaluation clocks — while a separate Facility Schools Board tightens who may open such a school at all.
Sources: - Colorado Department of Education, State Board release, September 11, 2026 (the department's three stated reasons for the rulemaking: recent legislation, a resolution agreement from a state complaint against the department, and stakeholder input) — verify by searching the CDE newsroom at cde.state.co.us for the September 2026 State Board release - Colorado Department of Education, November 2026 update to superintendents (hearing dates, testimony signup noon November 5 to noon November 11, and the rest of the November 12-13 agenda) — verify by searching the CDE site for the November 2026 update - Exceptional Children's Educational Act rules, redlined draft, October 2026 (draft sections 2.03, 4.02, and 8.06 of 1 CCR 301-8) — verify via the CDE Rulemaking page: search for 1 CCR 301-8 and open the redlined rules document - Colorado Department of Education, Office of Facility Schools, overview of approved facility schools and fiscal year 2025-26 tuition cost rates (34 schools, 923 students as of December 1, 2025; daily rates of 148, 215, and 307 dollars by category) — verify by searching the CDE Facility Schools pages - Chalkbeat Colorado, June 2026, reporting on the Facility Schools Board tightening proposal and the Westminster specialized day school — verify by searching chalkbeat.org/colorado for facility schools, June 2026 - Coloradoan, November 2026, Poudre School District special meeting and closure re-vote coverage — verify by searching coloradoan.com for the Poudre special meeting set for November 12, 2026

item.title: [Alaska] Deep Dive — Adequacy, in Writing: The Education Funding Task Force Draft
item.description:
Eighteen months after House Bill 57 created it, Alaska's Joint Legislative Task Force on Education Funding released its draft recommendations on November 9, 2026: adopt a legal definition of an adequate education, test the base student allocation against it — including what the flat special needs factor really buys for students with disabilities — fund schools on a three-year average enrollment, separate facilities money from classroom money against a five hundred thirty-five million dollar maintenance backlog, and keep the eighty-eight million dollar Energy Cost Reimbursement Program funded indefinitely. A complete walk-through of the formula, the adequacy cases behind it, the November 10 election count, and how to testify on November 12 or comment by December 8.
Sources: - Task Force on Education Funding, 'Education Task Force Releases Recommendations for Public Comment,' November 9, 2026 (alaskasenate.org — search 'Education Task Force Releases Recommendations for Public Comment'): adequacy definition, enrollment count update, full Energy Cost Reimbursement Program funding, maintenance revision; testimony November 12; written comments due December 8, 2026 to TFEF@akleg.gov or edfundtaskforce@akleg.gov; final report by the first day of the 2027 legislative session - Juneau Independent, 'Legislature's education task force seeks more funding via series of policy recommendations,' November 10, 2026 (juneauindependent.com): three-year average enrollment and the Juneau worked example (3,673 current vs. 3,971 average, nearly two million dollars, about eight percent); inflation adjustment; five hundred thirty-five million dollar maintenance backlog and quoted consequences; eighty-eight million dollar energy estimate; correspondence exemptions review; on-record statements by Tobin, Himschoot, Story, Kiehl, and Juneau Superintendent Shawn Arnold - Alaska Statutes Title 14, Chapter 17 (AS 14.17.410, 14.17.420, 14.17.470; law.justia.com — search 'Alaska Statutes 14.17.410 public school funding'): basic need formula; special needs factor 1.20; intensive services; base student allocation - Legislative Finance Division, K-12 Funding / Foundation Formula materials (akleg.gov — search 'Legislative Finance Division foundation formula BSA history'): school size factor range 1.13 to 3.30, district cost factor range 1.000 to 2.116, Fairbanks adjusted ADM example including 388 intensive students at thirteen times - House Bill 57 (2025), Laws of Alaska (akleg.gov — search 'HB 57 base student allocation task force'): BSA increase of seven hundred dollars from five thousand nine hundred sixty to six thousand six hundred sixty dollars; item.title: [New Mexico] Deep Dive — Incomplete, With a March Deadline: The Yazzie/Martinez Order
item.description:

item.title: [Indiana] Deep Dive — The Threat That Teaches: Indiana's Retention Research, the Law, and the IEP

item.title: [New Jersey] Deep Dive — When the Ceiling Fell: Lake Drive, a School for the Deaf, and the Education a Building Carries
item.description:
On November 3, 2026, part of a hallway ceiling collapsed during the school day at Lake Drive School in Mountain Lakes — the 112-year-old home of New Jersey's regional day program for deaf and hard of hearing students from more than 100 districts. No one was hurt. A week later the damage is long-term, over 100 students are split between two other schools, and a temporary alternate building is being sought. This deep dive covers what happened, what the Lake Drive Program is and why it exists, why the building itself is part of these students' IEPs and communication plans, what the law requires while a program is displaced, who pays to repair a historic schoolhouse in a regular operating district, and what the November 16 board meeting must decide.

item.title: [Puerto Rico] Deep Dive — When the Buses Stop: The Payment Collapse
item.description:
Puerto Rico's school buses stopped on November 10, 2026 — not for a strike, but because the Department of Education has not paid its carriers in months. item.title: [Texas] Deep Dive — The Money Arrived, the Rights Did Not: TEFA and Students with Disabilities
item.description:
A Houston-area family whose Texas Education Freedom Account placement collapsed weeks into the school year — a private school withdrew a child with autism and epilepsy over the outside therapy he could not attend without — opens the statewide pattern in the Comptroller's own data: more than thirty-three thousand eligible families opted out, most of them students with disabilities or the poorest qualifying families, nearly three hundred funded students already withdrawn, and an average disability award near sixteen thousand dollars against a thirty thousand dollar headline — alongside the state's own documents on what rights travel with the money and what stays behind.

item.title: [Guam] Deep Dive — Two Tracks, No Building Yet: The Simon Sanchez Restart
item.description:
Public Works announced November 9 that the Simon Sanchez High School project now moves on two tracks — demolition, cleared by the Attorney General and waiting on the Education Department to authorize its architect, and a public-private partnership construction package headed to the incoming administration — while neither demolition nor construction has begun. This deep dive gives the full history from Typhoon Mawar through the protested 167 million dollar procurement, what split sessions do to special education services and compensatory obligations, the 34.8 million dollar budget gap, the 113,503 dollar College Board balance, the sanitation-rule fight headed to the November 17 board meeting, and the two report-backs due today.

item.description:

item.title: [Idaho] Education Daily — November 12, 2026: A Judgment in Pocatello, and a Lab in Coeur d'Alene
